explanations.measures: The gap between reported profit and the cash actually collected, scaled by assets.
explanations.deterioration: Profit that never turns into cash is the oldest warning in accounting. The gap has to close eventually, usually by profit falling.
explanations.innocent: A company growing quickly funds working capital before it collects. Fast growth and early-stage contracts both widen the gap without anything being wrong.

explanations.measures: Whether money owed by customers, or stock on hand, is growing faster than sales.
explanations.deterioration: Customers paying more slowly, or stock that is not selling, often show up here before they reach the profit line.
explanations.innocent: Stock builds ahead of a genuine demand ramp or a new product launch, and a shift towards larger customers lengthens payment terms by agreement.

explanations.measures: Whether the number of shares is rising while the return on invested capital falls.
explanations.deterioration: Issuing shares into falling returns dilutes existing holders to fund something earning less than it used to.
explanations.innocent: A company issuing stock to fund an acquisition or a build-out will show lower returns while the investment is still being made.

explanations.measures: Whether goodwill, the premium paid over book value in acquisitions, is growing as a share of total assets.
explanations.deterioration: Goodwill is the asset most likely to be written off. A rising share means more of the balance sheet rests on deals having worked.
explanations.innocent: A company that has just made a large acquisition it will do perfectly well out of looks exactly like this.

explanations.measures: How much the tax rate moves around from year to year.
explanations.deterioration: A rate that jumps about can point to one-off items or aggressive positions holding up reported profit.
explanations.innocent: Where profits are earned changes, and one-off settlements and rate changes move the rate for entirely ordinary reasons.

explanations.measures: Whether pay issued in shares is growing as a share of revenue.
explanations.deterioration: Stock compensation is a real cost that does not leave the bank account. Rising fast, it flatters cash flow while diluting holders.
explanations.innocent: Competing for engineers means paying in stock. Plenty of good companies pay this way on purpose.

explanations.measures: Whether the company told the SEC it restated its accounts, changed auditor, or could not file on time in the last two years.
explanations.deterioration: These are not inferences. They are events the company disclosed itself, and they are the most direct evidence on this page.
explanations.innocent: Auditors are changed for cost and rotation rules, and a late filing can follow an acquisition or a system migration rather than a problem with the numbers.
